    Weekly Activity Sequences

    Overview

    There are four major activities in each week of DUTE_AI.  

    1) Complete core reading materials and pre-recorded lectures for the week.

    Every week there will be core readings (including further reading suggestions) and may be some pre-recorded lectures. Please aim to finish them before the class.

    2) Participate in a debate on the Moodle Forum

    Every week, you will be asked to join an online debate on a weekly proposed argument regarding the promises and challenges of educational technologies. You could either add comments for or against a weekly proposed argument using evidence from your readings, lectures, or personal experiences. Please engage in a debate on the Moodle Forum before the class (5 PM on Thursday UK time). 

    Each week, you will receive an  AI-generated first post when the weekly course content is released. These posts will be shared using the account named Yildiz Uzun.

    3) Attend a live class for the lectures and group activities

    Every week, a face-to-face class will be held at the room-G2 in the Knowledge Lab on Thursday at 5:00 PM (UK time). The live class comprises (1) a lecture (~90 mins) to answer some of the questions that you may have from the weekly materials, followed by (2) group activities (~90 mins).

    Throughout the module, you will be working on some learning analytics and AI tasks individually. In addition, you will work as a group on a data analytics project to tackle an educational problem. In relation to the weekly lecture content,  there will be tasks for you and your team to complete on Python Notebooks and Miro.

    Note: After interdisciplinary groups are formed based on your survey information, you will be invited to your group activity board on Miro. Please create an account on Miro using your real name and use the template to complete weekly group activities.

    For remote students, please see an additional guideline here.

    4) Reflect on Google Docs

    At the end of the week, you are expected to write your individual reflections on the weekly content/activities via a single Google Docs file. These reflections will be guided by specific questions posed each week.

    Please share your single Google Docs with us:

    • Qi Zhou ([redacted-contact])
    • Wannapon Suraworachet ([redacted-contact]) 
    • Yildiz Uzun ([redacted-contact])

    with editing access (editor) directly through emails. This only needs to be done once. 

    Here is general guidance on writing academic reflections.

    EducAItional Challenge Group Activity

    Throughout the module, you will be assigned to a group, and you will be asked to design, prototype, and evaluate machine learning solutions to address real-world educational challenges. This section covers information about how to approach the group work task.

    • EducAItional Challenge Group Activity Overview Page
    • Design Cases Page
  • Collapse Expand

    FAQ

    This section attempts to answer any questions that you may have.

    Learning Materials

    • When will the new week’s materials be released?

      • They are released every Monday for the following Thursday’s class.

    • Should I complete the video lectures and the essential reading before the class starts?

      • Yes, we are expecting you to prepare yourself before engaging with the class and the group activities. These materials are aimed to supply you with sufficient information to support your contributions during the class.

    • How can I have access to manuscripts, chapters, books etc.?

      • We are providing links to many readings. But, for others, you can search for articles using the UCL Explore library service: Go to Explore → Please see the instruction here: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/library/finding-resources/electronic-resources/about-explore 

    The Debate activity

    • Is this mandatory?

      • We strongly encourage you to contribute to the debate activity. It is also part of the attendance requirements, which requires you to engage with at least 80% of the module activities.

    • When is the deadline for this activity?

      • You are suggested to participate in the debate before the class starts on Thursday evenings. However, you can also respond to peers after class.

    Q&A sessions with the module instructor(s)

    • Is this mandatory?

      • Q&A sessions for online students are not mandatory. However, this session aims to open-up relevant discussion on the module content and help clarify questions that you might have so we suggest that you join us (besides they are often quite fun sessions!).

    • Will the Q&A sessions be recorded?

      • Yes, we will provide the link to the recordings afterwards.

    • What if I missed the session?

      • This is perfectly fine. If you have a question and couldn’t ask it during the session, you can always pose a question in the Moodle forum to ask us any time.

    Group Project

    • Do we have to create the design solution?

      • No, we only expect you to present the conceptual ideas of your design solution without a need to actually create one. However, you could include the prototypes of your design solution in the final presentation, if you have already started working on them.

    • Does the group project count as a part of the grade?

      • Yes, this activity is mainly aimed to help you develop an in-depth understanding of the contents through applied knowledge and collaboration. Both individual reflection portfolio and the critical essay submissions which are evaluated are directly related to your group work interactions, so doing a good job for your group work will matter for your grade. 

    • Does the Miro record count as a part of the grade?

      • We do not directly assess it. The tasks are designed to fuel you towards an understanding of the topic at hand and prepare you for your weekly reflections and the final submission.

    • When will the presentation take place?

      • In week 10, each group will present their design solutions case to the class. Groups can choose to present their idea in person or through a recorded video.

    • What is to be covered in the presentation?

      • We are expecting you to present a sensible flow of the weekly activities and developments that lead to your proposed solution to an educational challenge. 

    • Do I need to submit the presentation before the presentation day?

      • Yes, you are asked to submit your group presentation or video recording the day before the presentation day at 3 pm UK time. 

    • What will happen on the presentation day?

      • Each group will have 10 minutes to present, followed by 5 mins of a Q&A session. After every group has completed, everyone will vote for the top 3 design cases. The top team will receive a small gift from the module team. The voting system is only available synchronously during class time. Therefore, some remote students might not have a chance to cast their vote if they do not attend the session live.

    Weekly-surveys

    • Where can I access them?
      • Please create an account on the DUTE_AI App before logging in to submit your response. You might find this introduction to the app useful.
    • Is this mandatory?
      • They are not. This activity aims for students to reflect on their own conditions and possibly on other members’ conditions to foster group discussion and promote shared understanding within the group. 
    • What kind of data is collected?
      • The app only collects data about your email, your name and your group number. These data are stored in a real-time database (firebase) for the duration of your study for teaching and research purposes only and not shared further, deleted immediately after.
      • Apart from the surveys that you’ve submitted, the app also collects your log activity such as logging in/out, page viewing, and responses to the final survey questions. Please speak to a DUTE_AI team member if you have any questions.

    • When should I fill in the surveys?

      • The post-survey is expected to be completed right after the group discussion ended. However, both of the surveys will accept the responses at other times as well. 

    • Can I edit my response?

      • Currently, it is not possible to edit your responses. Please submit another response, we will consider the latest one as your intended response.

    • Who else can see my survey results?

      • Your surveys are only shared with your teammates to promote shared understanding.

    • Can I see my own response?

      • You are able to the follow-up plans from the surveys by selecting the 'My weekly goals/plan' from the menubar.

    • If I find errors in the app, what should I do?
      • Please send an email to [redacted-contact] , describing your process where it led to the errors and attaching a screenshot(s) of the errors. We will contact you to resolve the issue asap.

    Attendance requirements

    • How is this calculated?

      • UCL expects you to attend all scheduled teaching events and to be actively engaged in at least 80% of the module activities. The engagement is measured from your contributions to the debate activity, group discussions and the individual interaction data with the learning materials.

    • What will happen if I have to leave early for some weeks?

      • You are advised to inform the Module leader and the Teaching assistants when you are unable to attend a scheduled teaching event, or have to leave early. Moreover, for the module activities that are designed to be both synchronous and asynchronous, you can go back and complete any incomplete tasks at your preferred time. If you will not be able to attend multiple sessions, please submit a formal request for Extenuating Circumstances to the Department. Please see: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/academic-manual/chapters/chapter-2-student-support-framework/section-2-short-term-illness-and-other-extenuating 

    Assessment

    • Where can I find the example essays?

      • Please see under this section: example essays

    • What are the marking criteria?

      • Please see:  Marking Criteria File

    • What is the referencing style?

      • APA style is strongly suggested but any referencing style is acceptable, as long as it is consistently applied. Please refer to this page for more info: https://library-guides.ucl.ac.uk/APA

    • What would happen if the Turnitin results say that my final report is highly similar to my draft submission? Does it influence my final assessment? 

      • This wouldn't influence your final assessment as we can also see the similarity is with your own draft and differs from others’ work. 

    Part A Individual Reflection

    • What should be covered in my individual reflection?

      • In general, we are expecting you to reflect upon your learning experiences with the module ranging from the individual, group and cohort activities. We also provided weekly prompts under the weekly materials which you can consider while reflecting. However, please remember to cover the reflective contents across learning activities for each week. We are keen to know what you have learnt and how this has influenced your thinking, not a mere description of what happened during the class. 

    • How many words for the individual reflection weekly?

      • You are expected to provide a weekly reflection of approximately 300-500 words. However, the length of the document here is only a guideline as we don’t limit reflective writing. Longer writings for exceeding 500 words per week will only be evaluated for up to 500 words. Writing succinctly is an important skill to develop. There is no merit in lengthy submissions per se, but if you need space for more, the reasons why your reflections are greater than the suggested number of words should be justifiable.

    • Can I include a diagram(s) in the reflection document?

      • Yes if it helps convey your message. 

    • Do I need to add references to my individual reflections?

      • Yes, where possible, to show evidence for your arguments.

    • How should I share this part to receive feedback? Is there a deadline for this ?

      • Please use GoogleDocs as a documenting platform and share the document with teaching assistants as ‘editors’ via email once you created the document:

        • Qi Zhou ([redacted-contact])
        • Wannapon Suraworachet ([redacted-contact])
        • Yildiz Uzun ([redacted-contact])
    • Please update the contents weekly on the same document to receive analytics feedback. We will get in touch in case we have a problem with your document.

    • Since teaching assistants will provide formative feedback (in-text comments) as well during the reading week (week 6), it is suggested to keep your document updated by the time. However, this is optional. The final deadline for the summative assessment is the same deadline as Part B.

    • Can we revise it after receiving the comments?

      • We expect you to take the feedback on board and revise the contents of your reflection accordingly before the final deadline.

    • Do I need to create a new Google account for this?

      • You can either use your personal email or create a new google account using UCL email for this task specifically. In case you use your personal email, please make sure that we know who you are by including your name in the email or the document.

    • Which weeks are optional for reflection?

      • Week 1 and week 10 are optional for individual reflections

    • What is the format of the reflection document? When is the last day for editing my reflections? 

      • During the term, there is no specific format for the reflection other than the content and length to receive formative and analytics feedback. However, you need to submit your final version to the Moodle with your Part B- design critique, following the submission criteria.

    Part B Design Critique

    • What should be covered in the critical essay? Is it acceptable to choose one or two topics from the module (i.e. learning analytics, value-driven nature of data and algorithms, multimodal learning analytics, orchestration etc.) to go deeper into?

      • We anticipate coverage of all the topics delivered in DUTE_AI. However, it is perfectly normal that some weeks' content will be covered more in-depth, whereas some others will be more briefly mentioned.

    • Do I have to state which option I choose?

      • Not necessarily. We can infer this from your essay.

    • Option B.1 extending the group design case to a new problem: should I briefly describe my existing design?

      • Yes, as your essay is expected to be complete on its own. Please make sure that you include the necessary information on the existing design before starting to expand the design case. However, please note that what is expected is your critical evaluation of this new case rather than a descriptive discussion of the extension work.

    • Option B.2 critique of a technology design (commercial or academic) with respect to its educational value: Do I have to elaborate on whether I pick a commercial EdTech or an academic EdTech?

      • Not necessarily. You don't need to distinguish and try to build an argument whether the educational technology you are critiquing is an academic or a commercial one in your essay. We provide these options to keep students' opportunities wide so that everyone can write a critical essay on an EdTech they are genuinely interested in. The boundaries between the two are not very straightforward to draw. Many EdTech products start as academic/research products and can be later on commercialised (i.e Duolingo).

    Welcome to DUTE_AI 2025/2026!

    The content for face-to-face and remote students is equivalent. The only difference is in the delivery of the Q&A sessions and the group activities as elaborated below. The module is designed to provide the best learning experiences for both campus-based and remote students.

    Week 0: Get prepared! (Complete all by 29 Sep)

    Welcome to DUTE_AI 2025/2026!!

     

    Before the module lectures start, please pay attention to the following resources and activities that we've prepared for you. 

    Educational Technologies are important tools that can give teachers and learners a great deal of insight into the learning process. As much as we argue for the potential of educational technologies to support learning, we also think that all systems and decisions within educational technology implementations should be transparent to their users. Therefore, it is important that you know exactly what data you are generating through the technologies you are using in this module, how such data is utilised, and what kind of support we aim to provide you with the use of data. 

    For this induction week, we will present you with information about the types of data you will be generating through your engagement with the module and ask you to provide us with consent if you are happy to do so. Reading through these documents carefully and filling in the required information is extremely important for your optimised experience in the module and the following group activities. If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to get in touch for a discussion. 

    • There are 5 activities which you are required to complete before the start of week 1 lecture on Thursday:

      1. Read the Information sheet of research associated with this module. The module aims to provide a superior student experience with learning analytics interventions. You will be presented with the rationale behind the project and supportive information to opt-in to the project.

      2. Fill in the Consent Form: Please let us know the extent to which you agree/disagree to take part in the research aspects of the module. There are no obligations to consent. 

      3. Provide General Information about Yourself: This is a questionnaire regarding your background experience data which is crucial for us to formulate multidisciplinary, mixed-gender, and similar timezone groups for your group activities.

      4. Complete the SRL and Feedback Literacy questionnaires: These are questionnaires to gain some understanding of your self-regulatory behaviours and feedback literacy to better personalise and support your engagement at both individual and group level activities of the module. There are no right or wrong answers to these questions. 

      5. Introduction to tools: To help prepare you for the upcoming activities of the module, please familiarise yourselves with the listed tools, including Moodle, Miro, Google Docs and the DUTE_AI App (and Zoom for distance students). Please don't worry if you are new to these tools; you will have first-hand experience with them in week 1.

    Week 2: Data as the Key Affordance of Technology for Learning (w/c 06 Oct)

    Key Affordances of Technology for Learning: In this session, we will investigate the key affordances of technology for learning with a particular focus on data from educational technology and discuss to what extent technology can enhance learning. 

    Learning Outcomes

    • Consider data as a key affordance of technology to support and enhance the learning experience
    • Critically argue for or against the potential of data from technology to enhance learning
    • Learn simple regressors as models to process educational data

    Practical Skills: Using data for predictions with regression

    • Linear regression
    • Data transformation
    • Regression trees

    • Overview

      1) Reading task

      Please access them here: W2 Data as the Key Affordance of Technology for Learning

      2) Debate task

      This week's movement is "This House believes that technology, as a medium itself, does not enhance learning. Do you agree?" Click W2 Debate.

      3) Lecture

      In this lecture, we will discuss the role of data as a crucial affordance of technology in enhancing the learning experience. We will critically examine both the opportunities and limitations of using data from technology to improve learning, encouraging you to engage in a thoughtful debate on this subject. Additionally, we will introduce simple regression models, focusing on how these models can be used to process educational data for meaningful insights. By the end of the lecture, you will have gained practical skills in using data to make predictions through various regression techniques, including linear regression, data transformation, and regression trees, which are essential tools for analyzing and interpreting educational data.

      4) Team Discussion on your group design case

      This week you are asked to discuss prediction with linear regression, what features predict learning outcomes in your dataset and what are the limitations of the linear regression for predicting learning outcomes. 

      5) Individual reflection
      • What have you learned about the role of data as a key affordance of technology in supporting and enhancing learning?
      • What is your personal experience relevant to the module content, and how does it relate to the literature you read?
      • What did you learn from analysing your regression results, and how do these results show the impact of data on learning?

    Week 3: Richard Noss Lecture (w/c 13 Oct)

    Richard Noss Lecture 2025- Professor Manu Kapur

    "Learning Through Productive Failure In The GenAI Age"

    If learning from failure is intuitively compelling, why do we wait for it to happen. Why don’t we intentionally design for it, and harness it for deep learning? In his talk, Prof. Kapur will describe what Productive Failure is, how, when and why intentionally designing for failure in a safe way can lead to deep learning, and its implications for how we can design powerful learning environments for developing conceptual understanding, creativity, and transfer.

    Prof. Manu Kapur's lecture will be followed by a panel discussion:

    Panel Title: Human Learning and Generative AI: Neurocognitive Foundations, Pedagogical Innovation, & Technical Frontiers

    This panel will examine how generative AI is impacting higher education by interrogating the neurocognitive mechanisms underpinning learning, exploring genAI as a catalyst for learning and metacognition, and addressing the technical and research challenges in designing GenAI systems for nuanced pedagogical support for learning. Drawing on research and practice examples from UCL, ETH and beyond, panellists will debate what higher education should emphasise, how we scaffold learning, and what innovations are still needed.

    Week 5: Multimodal Learning Analytics (w/c 27 Oct)

    Multimodel learning Analytics: This week we will discuss the multimodality of learning and use multimodal data for advanced classification tasks. 

    Learning Outcomes

    • Explore different modalities of data that can be used to model and support learning
    • Identify the advantages and challenges of taking a multimodal approach to the design and use of learning analytics
    • Learn advanced data analytics approaches to prediction modelling with multimodal data

    Practical Skills: Advanced approaches to predictions

    • Algorithm assembling 
    • Decision trees
    • Bagging approach with Random Forest
    • Boosting approach with XGBoost (theoretical)

    • Overview

      Key Activities

      1) Reading task

      Please access them here: https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/mod/book/view.php?id=7651064&chapterid=207849 

      2) Debate task

      This week's movement is "This House believes that, in educational technology, the benefits of multimodal data outweigh its challenges. Do you agree?" Click W5 Debate.

      3) Lecture

      Educational research has revealed the pedagogical benefits of letting students experience different types of content, "real world" challenges, and physical and social interactions with educators or other learners. This is partly because students' learning happens in situ, where the learner is. Learning is not necessarily constrained to a specific physical space (e.g. the classroom) or a digital environment (e.g. an institutional learning management system or a specific learning digital tool). Students commonly work outside the boundaries of the institutional learning system(s). This inherently blended nature of learning settings makes it essential to move beyond educational technologies that rely solely on a single data source (e.g. log files) or that focus only on the interactions that occur between learners and a specific system without considering the context of use. In this week's lecture, we will focus on multiple modalities that can be taken into account to provide continued support for learning across physical and digital spaces.

      4) Team Discussion on your group design case

      This week you will be asked to do advanced classifications with multimodal data and discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the multimodal data for your group design case.

      5) Individual reflection

      • What are the promises and challenges of using multimodal data in learning technologies? How might multimodal data apply to your group's design case? 

      • What are the potential benefits and limitations of using advanced classification approaches (e.g. Random Forest and XgBoost) with multimodal data in educational contexts?

      • Reflect upon the analytics feedback you received on different sections: individual feedback, group processes and group challenges/regulation. What did you think their strengths were? What were the limitations? Did they help you change your learning behaviours? How could the feedback be improved to help you more?

      This week's lecture will discuss the value-driven nature of artefacts including educational technologies and will argue for learning sciences driven educational technologies. This week, we will investigate the 'politics' of educational technologies and discuss the potential underlying values that shape the design and use of technology in education. Using case study examples, we will build up the arguments for potential values that could/should be driving educational technologies for learning.

    Week 7: From Prediction to Generation | Natural Language Processing in Education (w/c 17 Nov)

     

    From Prediction to Generation | Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Education: Building on the previous week’s prediction models, this session extends predictive thinking to analyse and generate text-based data through Natural Language Processing. We introduce how machines represent language—from BoW and TF-IDF to embeddings and LLMs—and compare their performance on educational tasks such as essay scoring.

    Learning Outcomes

    • To understand the fundamentals of natural language processing, how machines process and represent language, from traditional NLP (BoW, TF-IDF, word2vec) to modern LLMs, and how they have been used for educational tasks.
    • To learn key NLP techniques, including preprocessing and embeddings for analysing and generating educational text data.

    Practical Skills: Structure Discovery and Information Generation

    • Building basic NLP pipelines with BoW, TF-IDF, and Word2Vec (Recurrent Neural Network).

    • Overview

      Key Activities

      1) Reading task

      Please access them here: https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/mod/book/view.php?id=7651064&chapterid=207856



      2) Debate task

      This week's movement is "This House believes that all knowledge required for teaching and learning can be accurately represented by AI models acting as tutors. Do you agree?" Click W7 Debate. 

      3) Lecture

      Please visit an optional lecture by Prof. Mutlu on W3 on the introduction to neural networks and large language models HERE.

      Consider the vastness of knowledge and the complexities of teaching and learning: can we truly encapsulate all of it in AI models, even as advanced as recent GPT-based AI tutors? On one side, AI in education promises to adapt according to evidence-based learning principles (see the video lecture and reading, for instance), data-driven insights, and scalable support. Yet, the art of teaching involves nuance, empathy, and adaptability—qualities often seen as uniquely human. AI models may replicate structured knowledge and provide responsive feedback, but can they truly capture the depth of human experience and adapt to the unique needs of every learner? Does it even matter that they are fundamentally different from human tutors if they are to deliver expected learning outcomes on certain objectives on content acquisition and skills development? 

      4) Team Discussion on your group design case

      This week, you are asked to meet with your group and work on an NLP task, building and comparing the performance of three NLP pipelines (TFIDF, Doc2vec and Llama) for an essay scoring task. You can find the details of the NLP task in W7 Group Activities- Dataset & Script.

      With AI’s ability to understand human language and act as a tutor, you will begin envisioning how your group’s design case should look in terms of interfaces and interactions. Next week, you will build on this design to support meaningful human–AI interactions aimed at achieving synergy.

      Optional task: We have also prepared a script for building a neural network and comparing its performance with the other predictive models developed in earlier weeks for your group design case in W7 Group Activities- Dataset & Script.

      5) Individual reflection

      • How can the concepts and techniques you’ve learned this week, such as NLP and generative AI be applied to enhance your design case and your practice?

      • How have you engaged with this week’s content, and what more can you do to deepen your understanding and application of these concepts?

    Week 8: AI and a Vision for Hybrid Intelligence Systems (w/c 24 Nov)

    Three conceptualisations of AI in Education: This lecture will challenge the prevalent narrow conceptualization of AI as stochastic tools, highlighting two common fallacies in current discourse about AI’s transformative potential in education. The lecture delves into three conceptualizations of AI in education: the externalization of cognition, the internalization of AI models to influence human thought processes, and the extension of human cognition via tightly integrated human-AI systems.

    Learning Outcomes

    • Broaden your definition of artificial intelligence and extend your thinking beyond the 'externalisation' of human cognition with AI
    • Be familiarised with the approaches to prompt engineering of GenAI in Education
    • Understand differences in teacher-AI teaming and their potential impacts on human learning

    Practical Skills: Engineering prompts for essay marking

    • Using API to access foundational models
    • Prompt-tune a model for a specific educational purpose

      Please access them here: https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/mod/book/view.php?id=7651064&chapterid=207851

      2) Debate task

      This week's movement is "This House believes that AI and Analytics interventions should always be driven by evidence of impact from the research literature. Do you agree?" Click W9 Debate.

      3) Lecture

      There is an increasing emphasis on ‘evidence‐based teaching’ and 'evidence-based education'. The evaluation of educational technologies is important for their impacts to be effectively integrated into learning and teaching settings to bring the best benefit to learners and teachers. However, the impact evaluations of technology in education are challenging and what is 'evidence' in educational contexts is not an easy question to answer. These challenges are more significant for emerging technologies with genAI models. In this week's lecture, we will discuss the complexities of evaluating the impact of an AI intervention in Education. 

      4) Team Discussion on your group design case

      This week, you are asked to meet with your group and conduct a benchmarking study to evaluate genAI performance. Also, you will use a logic model to evaluate the potential solution of your group design case solution with AI. 

      5) Individual reflection

      • What have you learned about the importance of generating evidence for the effectiveness of AI implementations in education?

      • What challenges do you foresee in evaluating the performance of generative AI tools in education?

      • Reflect on how the GenAI assistant implemented on DUTEApp shaped your engagement with the analytics feedback, drawing on the ideas about evidence-informed AI in Education and the challenges of evaluating GenAI. How did it impact your learning, and what changes would make it a more effective learning partner for interpreting and acting on your analytics feedback?

    Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)

    Student presentations: In this session, you will present your group challenge which you put into practice and illustrate different methods, concepts and ideas explored with the design and use of AI.

    • Overview

      Key Activities

      1) Team Discussion on your group design case

      This week's group meeting is optional, in case you want to meet as a group and discuss the organisation of your group presentation before it is presented or reflect upon how it went after your presentation.  

      2) Share your group work video
      Instructions for presentation preparations, timings and deadlines
      Prepare a presentation lasting up to 10 minutes. You can use PowerPoint or other means (drama, role-play, video, animation) to visually support your presentation.

      • If you are not able to present your work, students are asked to send a short video presentation of their group work. 
      • Please submit a copy of your presentations on Moodle by 11/12/2025 Thursday, 10 am.

      The slide/video presentations should mainly cover the below points;

      • State your solution designed and explain the motivation behind the choice. Provide a clear definition of the problem you have identified within the design case. What is the problem your AI or LA technology solution is trying to solve?
      • What is the specific AI/LA solution you are proposing? What is the specific methodology used to create your AI/LA solution and what theoretical approaches to learning are used to underpin it?
      • What is the expected impact of your proposed solution, and how will your AI/LA solution achieve this impact? (What are the outputs and outcomes you aim to measure?)

      3) Individual reflection

      • What have you learned from working as a group in this module?,  What went very well during the module?
      • What would you do in order to get more out of the module?, What are your goals for the next module?
      • What will you take from this module to implement in other modules you will take in the future and your learning in general?

    Assessment and Submission (Final submission due 7th January 2026 by 13:00)

    Assessment guidance and instructions for submission 

    • Guidance

      All assessment for DUTE_AI  follows the assessment guidance covered in the Programme Handbook for Staff and Students (available on the MA Education and Technology Programme Hub page on Moodle). 

      Any questions about the general assessment regulations or the assessment for this module can be directed to the Programme Leader, or the DUTE_AI Module Leader. 
       
      Students are responsible for reading and understanding all of the content in the Programme Handbook as well as the Module Handbook here. 
       
      Academic Writing Statement
       

      Pieces of work are marked in accordance with the marking criteria. There is no bell curve of marks or limits on the numbers of particular grades. Each piece is marked individually. Students are advised to take very careful note of the marking criteria used for DUTE_AI below.

      Students are welcomed and encouraged to write in the first person (i.e. to use I think...). Personal opinions are valid contributions but must be understood as only one person's experience and viewpoint, and thus cannot stand as a sole piece of evidence for an argument. 

      Although APA style is strongly suggested, any referencing style is acceptable, as long as it is consistently applied. If you are unsure of referencing, please consult the provided guide. 

      The final submission of work in Part A has no total word limit, but it is recommended to keep each week's reflections to around 500 words. 

      The final submission of work in Part B should be within +/- 10% of the word count. Pieces shorter than this are unlikely to meet the marking criteria and will likely score poorly because of this. Pieces that are longer than this will likely fail to deliver the ideas succinctly. The markers try very hard to mark and provide sensible feedback within a reasonable timeframe. Wordcounts help us to do this - so please don't go over! Writing concisely and editing are also important skills to learn.

      The final submission file should include both Part A and Part B assignments combined as a single file.

    • Submit your final assessment here. Due Wednesday 7th January 2026 by 13:00 (UK time). Please also submit here if you have an EC, DAP or Reasonable Academic Adjustment (extension). Assignment

      You must submit a single Microsoft Word document as the final assignment including the coversheets for Part A and Part B as the first four pages of your assignment followed by Part A and Part B. Use the coversheet file provided above this submission box.  Do not use any coversheets that you have previously used for other assignments.

       All submissions must conform to these requirements:

      • Submit as a Microsoft Word document.
      • Written work needs to be in a font size 12 and in New Times Roman font. 
      • 1.5 line spacing.  
      • Include page numbers. 
      • Include a word count (please note that the word count excludes the abstract, footnotes, bibliography/references list, appendices and title).
      • Remove any track changes or comments from the assignment.
      • You must tick the student declaration box confirming that this is your work. This is a UCL requirement.
      • For Part B, please be aware that you must be within the word count range and must not be greater or less than 10% than the stated word count. Work that exceeds the word count by more than 10% will be reduced by one grade (although this must not take the mark below the pass mark).  There are no penalties for any submissions which are under the word count
      • Do not put your name or student number anywhere on the document

      *** Your assignment title must be your candidate number followed by the title of your submission ***

      Student Candidate Number  

      To find your candidate number log into your PORTICO account, go to “My Studies” then the “Examinations” container. Your candidate number will be a combination of four letters plus a number (Example: ABCD9).  It is different to your student number (which is numeric). Please note that if you are a part-time or flexible student, your candidate number changes each year. 

      Checking your work on Turnitin before you submit

      If you would like to get a 'similarity report' on your assignment before you submit it,  please visit https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/enrol/index.php?id=34 and log in with your UCL username and password. Then click the 'Enrol me' button and select 'Check Your Work with Turnitin' tab. 

      If you need help understanding Turnitin, we advise you to click on ‘Student Help’ and then ‘Moodle Student Guides’ and then ‘Turnitin assignment for submission and feedback’ from the top menu on the Home Moodle page. There are lots of pages of advice there, including a Turnitin FAQ.
